blocks.text: 1.5.1 instanceof Operator in Java

A service loads each plugin through a class loader of its own. The first request to a plugin fails with `ClassCastException: class Greeter cannot be cast to class Greeter`, and the `instanceof Greeter` test a line earlier was `false`, though both classes have the same name and the same bytecode.
Pattern variables are unit 1.5.2; record patterns and `switch`, units 1.5.3 and 1.5.4.
instanceof Asks About the Object's Class at Run Time, and null Has None
A YAML reader filled this configuration map:

retries instanceof Integer: false
(Integer) retries: null
timeout instanceof Number: true, Comparable: true, Integer: false
Number.class.isInstance(timeout): true
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because "retries" is null

The test ignores the declared type, `Object` here, and asks whether the class of the object the variable refers to is `T` or a subtype of `T`. A `Long` is a `Number` and a `Comparable`, never an `Integer`. `null` refers to no object, so the test is `false` for every `T`. `Class.isInstance` is the same test with the type as a value.

The cast disagrees on `null`. It checks the class and throws `ClassCastException` on a mismatch (unit 1.1.3), but it lets `null` through, so the missing key surfaces later, as a `NullPointerException` where the `Integer` is unboxed. Test a value that may be absent before casting it.
A Class Is Its Name and the Loader That Defined It
The plugin from the start of the unit, reduced: a `URLClassLoader` with no parent defines its own `Greeter` from the same class file the application loaded.

class name: Greeter
greeter instanceof Greeter: false
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException: class Greeter cannot be cast to class Greeter (Greeter is in unnamed module of loader java.net.URLClassLoader @5c647e05; Greeter is in unnamed module of loader 'app')

At run time the JVM identifies a class by its name and the loader that defined it. The caller's `Greeter` is the application loader's, so the plugin's object is of an unrelated class. A cache that keeps objects across a reload hands out instances of the old classes. Load the shared type from a parent loader both sides use, or drop the old objects with the old loader.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Compiler Rejects a Test That Can Never Be True, Judging Only the Declared Types

Impossible.java:5: error: incompatible types: Integer cannot be converted to String
Impossible.java:7: error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Runnable
Impossible.java:8: error: incompatible types: int[] cannot be converted to Object[]
Impossible.java:9: error: incompatible types: Integer cannot be converted to String

javac accepts `x instanceof T` only if a cast from `x`'s declared type to `T` could succeed for some object. No object is both an `Integer` and a `String`. A `Thread` can be a `List`, since a subclass of `Thread` may implement it, so the `worker` test compiles and is decided at run time. `String` is `final`, as are `Integer` and `Long`, and it doesn't implement `Runnable`, so no subclass can add it. The cast follows the same rule.
Against an `Object` parameter every test compiles, even one no caller can satisfy.
**Primitive types.** Java 21 rejects `x instanceof Integer` for an `int x`: the left side must be a reference. Java 25's javac reports it as a preview feature ("primitive patterns").
<!-- practice 4 -->
Arrays Keep Their Element Type at Run Time; Generic Types Lose Their Type Arguments

names: Object[] true, String[] true
untyped: String[] false
counts: Object[] false, Object true
java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer
payload instanceof List<?>: true
cast done, size 2
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (java.lang.Integer and java.lang.String are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')

An array's class is fixed when it is created, whatever it holds later: `untyped` holds only strings and is still no `String[]`. A `String[]` is also an `Object[]`, and the array checks every store, hence the `ArrayStoreException`. An `int[]` holds no references, so it is an `Object` but not an `Object[]`.

A generic type keeps no type argument at run time: `ArrayList<String>` and `ArrayList<Integer>` are one class. The cast to `List<String>` could check only `List`, and javac flags it only as unchecked. The `ClassCastException` comes from a cast the compiler inserted at `tags.get(0)`, in whatever code reads the list, as with the varargs array in unit 1.3.2. For the same reason javac refuses `payload instanceof List<String>` for an `Object payload`:
GenericTests.java:7: error: Object cannot be safely cast to List<String>

Since Java 16 a type argument is allowed where the declared type already guarantees it: `tags instanceof ArrayList<String>` compiles for a `List<String> tags`. Before that, only a raw type or `<?>` was. To get a `List<String>` out of an `Object`, test `List<?>`, then test every element.
<!-- practice 2 -->
In equals, instanceof Breaks Symmetry With a Subclass, and getClass() Refuses Every Subclass
Unit 1.3.4 fixed an `equals(Sku)` overload with an `equals(Object)` that starts with a type test. Here both classes test with `instanceof`, and the subclass adds a field:

Output for `depot = new Point(3, 4)` and `gate = new LabeledPoint(3, 4, "gate B")`, then with `if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;` in place of each `instanceof` line, then against an anonymous `new Point(3, 4) { }`:

instanceof:  depot.equals(gate) true, gate.equals(depot) false
             List.of(depot).contains(gate) false, List.of(gate).contains(depot) true
             HashSet size, depot added first 2, gate added first 1
getClass():  depot.equals(gate) false, gate.equals(depot) false
             depot.equals(subclass adding nothing) false

`Object.equals` requires symmetry: `x.equals(y)` is true exactly when `y.equals(x)` is. `depot` accepts any `Point`; `gate` only a `LabeledPoint`. `contains` calls `equals` on its argument, so `contains` answers differently depending on which of the two the list holds, and a `HashSet` keeps one or both depending on which was added first.

`getClass()` restores symmetry by refusing every other class, even a subclass that adds no field. A `final` value class avoids the choice, since `instanceof` is then exact; every record is final. When a type needs more state, hold a `Point` in a field instead of extending it.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **`instanceof` tests the run-time class of the object, subtypes included, and is `false` for `null`.** A cast lets `null` through, and a class is its name plus its loader, so a reloaded class is a different type.

**The compiler rejects a test that can never be true, from the declared types only.** An interface test compiles unless the class is `final` and doesn't implement it; an `Object` parameter turns the check off.
**Arrays know their element type; generics don't.** An `int[]` is not an `Object[]`, and an unchecked cast to `List<String>` fails later, where an element is read.
**In `equals`, `instanceof` with a subclass that adds state breaks symmetry; `getClass()` refuses all subclasses.** Make value classes `final`, or compose instead of extending.

Challenges

items: Your service decodes JSON into `Map<String, Object>`. Find every cast that follows a `get` and decide which should test, which should fall back to a default, and which should fail loudly.
A library's class hierarchy uses `instanceof` in `equals`. You must subclass it and add a field. What are your options, and what does each cost?
How does your framework's development-mode restart load your classes, and which cached objects could outlive a restart?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Java Lets Code Ask an Object's Class

Polymorphism is the usual way to vary behavior by type: each class overrides `area()`, and the caller calls it. A chain of `instanceof` tests does the same from outside the classes and must be edited for every new subtype; one it misses falls to the `else` without a warning. Java still needs the test where code receives an object whose type nobody could declare: `equals(Object)`, deserialized data, a plugin. Sealed types with a `switch` (unit 1.5.4) bring the compiler back into such a chain, which then fails to compile when a subtype is added and not handled.
